utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berghofer. If I could you mind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I want to move on in our evidence, please, to your return to Velepromet on the 21st of November. Now, can we just deal with your return. Do you remember coming back to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you've told us that you came back, I think, with the same people who had been with you to Modateks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with Velepromet. Were you actually taken inside or did you go inside the Velepromet facility?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out from Modateks across the field. We actually walked across the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you have -- did you travel by yourselves or did you have any escort or people with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were escorted by Jezdimir Stankovic, who was the brother of a friend of mine and another man. They were wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And just for completeness, were they armed or not? That's Stankovic and the other.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They had automatic rifles. And he said: Don't run away, Beli, otherwise we'll have to kill you. I was the first, and all the others were following behind me. He didn't say anything else bad. He didn't kick me or anything. Then we entered Velepromet. We entered a room, but in front of that room there were two young regular soldiers. They searched me. They took my watch and very few Yugoslav dinars that Goran Ivankovic gave to me in Modateks. There wasn't a whole lot, just a little bit. But the soldier who took my watch said: This is the kind of thing I like. And he said: What do you have in your shoes? I had new walking shoes. And I said: I have nothing. And he said: If I find anything at all, I'll cut your feet off. And I said: Okay. So that was all the conversation I had with them, and then we entered the room and it was the so-called death chamber. Whoever went in never used to come out alive; that's why we used to call it a death chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I'd just like you, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if it's possible for the registry to put on the screen a photograph, aerial photograph, of the Velepromet facility. The number is 04672115. Now, can that be blown up, please, so that we can see it. Mine's not very well in focus, but let's try it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is a photograph, Mr. Berghofer, of the Velepromet facility from the air. Now, have you got it in focus, or is it, like mine, rather opaque, rather blurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's pretty clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On your left-hand side, I believe, perhaps even on your right-hand side, we have got a screen and we have got a magic pencil that allows you to mark up and to point out where you were taken. Now, before you do that, because you've not done this before, just look at the facility, familiarise yourself with it. The -- the entrance is to the right, as we look at the photograph. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you put a small cross and an A, a capital A where the entrance is, as you understand it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you've told us that you were taken to a room. Can you circle the area where the room is, as far as you believe it to be. So can you put a circle around the area where the room is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you put an R for that, please, standing for "room."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: But could we make that a little bigger, do you think?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder if I might make a suggestion to the Court, whether it's possible for the assistant to put a clear letter to assist all parties when it comes to the recollection, to put an R there. I don't know if the Court would agree with that proposed course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I see at the moment an R that's reasonably clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I've got a very bad screen, so I can't see anything apart from red. If it's clear for all parties, then there's no problems about that. Might I then ask for that to be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest if the court officer would put a capital A at the first marking. THE USHER: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 229.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we just switch off that particular exhibit, please, from the screen? And can I be told when that's been removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So that particular map has now gone, has it? Is it still there, Mr. Berghofer, or has it been removed or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's not been removed? It's gone now. Very well. Let's deal then, please, with your evidence about the room. Why did you call it the room of death?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we came across some of ours, some of my acquaintances, such as Ljubo Pribudic [phoen], Slobodan Vuletic. The young Uhlarik, Crk, who was the manager of the Vukovar slaughter-house. Rene Matausek. Another young guy who was Golac's son, and Golac was a friend of mine. And then there were two women there as well. And then there was this son of a Roma musician there as well. And an elderly friend of mine as well; I can't remember his family name right now. Then another two women and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt you. Can you -- if you want to carry on, do carry on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those of us who arrived from Modateks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you say you came across some of ours, were those people actually inside the room when you entered that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, yes. They were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Were you able to see if any of them or injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The young Uhlarik and Slobodan Vuletic were tied up with wire, their hands and their backs. And the others were not tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, what happened when you were in that room.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We arrived at around 3.30. It was still day-light and it was a nice day. And as time went on, a reservist came in. He was uniformed. He was a local. And if Your Honours allow me -- I mean, he used rather vulgar language. Am I free to repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't think there's any problem. Most people, I think, have heard bad language.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That person, a young man, about 28, 29 years of age, a stout man, blond, he turned to Miroslav Perkovic and said: Fuck your mother. Did you need this? And he hit him with a heavy shoe on his head. And he said: First I'll cut your ears off and then your head as well. And he got that young Roma guy Dzemo, the gypsy's son, he got him up. He was a short guy, no more than a metre and a half, as we used to say. And this other guy was a powerful, a strong man. So he lifted him up basically, and he said: This is a real ZNG and not you. And he took Rene Matausek, and Dzoga, Crk, and his manager, because they used to work together in the same company, the four of them as I remember now, and then he came back for Miroslav Perkovic. And he kicked him twice and he threw him out, pushed him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with the way you describe certain things. You use the phrase "he came back for Perkovic." Now, to come back in my language means to have gone out and returned.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, what did he do then with the others before he came back for Perkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took him out -- he took them out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever see the people that he took out of the room? Did you ever see them again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never again, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The people who were in the room when you entered - and you've described and given the names of some of those people - what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, well, if you take the Roma boy and, to be quite honest, Slobodan Vuletic was raised by a man who wasn't his parent or anything, so he never knew what his real nationality was, at least I myself was never interested to find out. And all the others were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You've told us about people being taken out and Perkovic being kicked. What other incidents happened in that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- room that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he slapped this elderly friend of mine quite forcefully. He was born maybe in 1936 more or less. And as far as I can remember, another man who I knew by sight very well, an elderly gentleman, he was complaining that he left his wife at home and she was bedridden and that she was on her own for four days by then. And he used to live next to the Sloga football stadium. And he was asking to be allowed to go and see her and at least be able to give her a drink of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you remember coming out of the room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, how that occurred? What happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I need to give you a very brief introduction to this bit. When they were taken out, a neighbour of mine came along. His name -- his mother's family name was Ikac and his father's family name was Turukalo. Up until the 16th, we had been giving him food. He was a Serb, an Orthodox man, and he never participated in any sort of action. He never did anything wrong, but on the 21st he was already wearing a uniform and an automatic weapon. He came in and with a smirk on his face he said: Oh, look who's there. And another one said: Beli, I wouldn't like to be in your shoes. And I asked: Why not? And he said: For all the tales you told on Radio Vukovar. And I said to him: I didn't tell tales. I am Beli and not Bili. Bili was the mayor. And that was the end of the story. And at around 11.00, 11.30 p.m., the door opened and two young soldiers came in. And they said: Don't be afraid; the captain wants to save you. Let's go out. And we then went out and we pushed the bus, because the engine wouldn't start, and finally it did start and we were driven to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let us deal then, please, with the barracks. How many people from that room were taken to the JNA barracks that evening? Just give us an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe some 50 [as interpreted] people. Some of them came from some other rooms, I can't tell you exactly where from, but there were not that many of us in that one room that I was referring to earlier. There were more people on the bus than in the room, so they must have come from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one point with regard to the transcript. Page 8, line 13, the witness said "15 people," and it has come out as "50" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just check that, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, there may be a difficulty in the translation sometimes. I just want to clarify one small matter. We don't know whether you said it was either 15, 1-5, or 5-0, 50, people who went to the barracks. Can you clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Berghofer has never said "50" because there had never been 50 people there. Between 13 and 15, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, let's deal, please, if we may, with over at the barracks. Where were you taken -- where were you taken to, inside the barracks or outside the barracks? Can you give us a picture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the barracks, in a room there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were all of you in the same room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened in the barracks, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as we entered the room, we got a pack of cigarettes and a can of meat. The manufacturer was the Gavrilovic company. And we were given 250 grams of bread; as we say, a quarter of a kilo of bread. I, myself, had had nothing to eat for three days, and I suppose it was the same for the others. When we had eaten, a gentleman came in. He had a huge beard. It covered most of his face. I don't suppose his own mother would have known him had she seen him. He lined us up, and he started giving us a political lecture. He said: What for did you serve the Ustashas? Wasn't this state good enough for you? And so on and so forth. I must admit, I couldn't remember everything he said. He didn't actually hit anyone, but he insulted us a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said that "he didn't actually hit anyone." Was anyone hit in the barracks when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We nodded off for a minute, and I heard sounds of someone being hit and I heard someone moan. As far as I remember, the person being hit was my neighbour Silt, but we never talked about this later. I don't see that many people really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say it was your neighbour, does that mean he was in the same room as you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have no idea where he came from. I can't say. He was in the same room, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you actually see who was hitting him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think the time came when you eventually left the JNA barracks. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The next morning, the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you very briefly, so that we get a picture of what happened, tell us how it was you eventually left the barracks.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning a young soldier came and said: Your full name and your ethnicity. There were two or three ethnic Serbs there. I remember one man who's name was Zare. He was suffering from some sort of mental disturbance or deficiency. All the others there were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened then, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say -- I've always been a Croat myself, ever since I was born. But then the census came along at one point, and my former wife, my ex-wife, was an Orthodox lady, a Ruthenian, and when the census came, it was for our children's sake that she wrote Yugoslav ethnicity. My last name happens to be very difficult to spell, and I was the last to enter my name, so I told the soldier: Drago, Berghofer, Yugoslav. 40 minutes later he came back and said: I'll be calling out names, and those whose names are called out must go to the bus. When he came to me he said: A Yugoslav. So we got on the bus, and we were off to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the people who went to Sremska Mitrovica, what was the ethnicity of those people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a man name Slobodan Nikolic among us, a rather young man. He liked football, but he liked a good drop, too. I called him Stoplara, and he got on the bus at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, that's obviously the way I put the question. The people who got on the bus that morning from the JNA barracks, can you tell us what ethnicity they were, the bus that went to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question perfectly well, sir. That's what I was trying to point out. He was the only Serb to get on that bus; all the rest of us were Croats. Had he been at the barracks, he would not have been on that same bus with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to deal with probably only two other topics. We know, because we've heard in this court, that there were various wells in the Vukovar city area. Now, were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about the wells, especially those in my immediate surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the wells themselves - you excuse the pun - how well were they known to the general population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 40 years ago, nearly every house had a well. There were five or six wells in Stjepan Radica Street alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you -- do you know from your personal knowledge of what -- from what you've been told whether the administration ever kept a check on the wells before 1991? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us then what you know about the administration's knowledge of the wells.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1990 or thereabouts, they started listing all the wells. My house was near the barracks, and we didn't have a well. However, 300 metres down the street there was another house with a well outside in the streets, and the opening was covered over in concrete. I said: Let's keep this one. And my shop was nearby, just down the street. But the wells were targeted by mortars with such precision that they were all destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. I want to deal with an area --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we could show the map, the large map. I think it's Exhibit 170, but it's map 6. It's Exhibit 156. Can we show that on the screen? It's 0462-6622.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, again we're going to hope that it will come on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just say that the screen here in this court that I have is always causing problems for both Mr. Smith and myself. We don't have a clear picture. I wonder if it's possible for the administration to have a look at it at some time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure that can be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We like to keep the Prosecutors very vague and somewhat in the dark, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's a natural gift in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, do you have a map in front of you on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you actually see it clearly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can see the hospital. You can see Velepromet. You can see the road to Ovcara, the road to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, what I would like done, please, if it's possible - and I'll move to this screen, if I may, which is better - I would like to see if the administration, the registry, could focus in to what I call the central area, please, the Americans call "downtown." Yes. I hope that's clearer for everybody. Now, can I just go through this map with you, Mr. Berghofer. If you look at the map you can see lines running from top to bottom. The top is the north; the bottom is the south, and obviously lines across going east and west. You have got a large area of blue going through this map, which I know you have seen before, and that is the Danube. And then you have the Vuka river which runs almost at right angles, coming out almost where the N is of Dunav. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to put a small red dot where you believe the Vuka River comes out into the Danube.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I want to deal with the area that is south of the Vuka River, where the vast majority of the buildings are. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, by common consent, that is the principal part of Vukovar, the residential area itself. Do you agree or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us how badly damaged that area was from September, October, through to November. Can you give a description to the Court the sort of damage that was being done south of the Vuka River.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- not that I think, I actually passed there earlier on, too. The road I usually took was to the hospital and back. Everything was flattened. I couldn't see a building that was still intact anywhere along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I want to deal with damage or injury to civilians in the area south of the Vuka River, the area that I've referred to. I think it's right to say that you had a common-law wife in 1991? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you these questions, but I'm afraid I have to. And what was her name, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubica Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what happened to her?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was living -- I'm not sure how I should explain that to you. It was some distance from my house, but the same general direction. The road leading past the barracks. It was an area called two hills. That was where she lived. They shelled the entire area, so she fled to Radiceva Street and stayed at number 74. She took shelter in my cellar with another 40 women and children. That was in my shop, and the cellar I had at Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So how did she die, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Every single day the shelling was so heavy that you just couldn't keep track anymore. There was a shell that landed in the courtyard. It shattered all the glass panes, smashed against the concrete wall of the shop, and the cellar was in the same building. She didn't want to light a cigarette down in the cellar, so she just popped her head out for a minute, and she was struck in the neck by shrapnel, by a piece of shrapnel. She was killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you that, but I haven't quite finished. You also had a daughter who unfortunately was killed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court in very short form how it was you believe she was killed. And you don't have to go into detail. Just shortened form is fine.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met my grandchild, that was four years later, in Blace, which was a refugee camp, my granddaughter told me that Cvijanovic Pavle had taken her away, a man, a Serb, whom we had been giving food to up until the 17th. Whenever my ex-wife met him, she would ask him the same thing every time: Where's my daughter? Can I use some foul language, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Go fuck yourself. That was his reply every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, when it was, before or after the fall of Vukovar, that you believe she was killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was taken to Negoslavci to stay with someone who was allegedly a relative, or maybe she was evacuated to that area. So for a while he stayed at Negoslavci. All I knew was she had been taken away. Pavo Gavric, who was at this time taken to Mitrovica, when they took her to Negoslavci at more or less the same time, once he had left Mitrovica he said that my daughter had been taken to Negoslavci. This was on the 15th of September or thereabouts. However, she went back. She went back to the house after the fall of Vukovar, and it was sometime in early December that she was eventually led away, on the 1st or 2nd of December. I can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry to ask you those questions. Finally this: We have -- I want to return to the list, and I'd like you to be given a hard copy, please, 04680147. It was made an exhibit yesterday. Now, can we just deal with this list. Mr. Berghofer, you've told us that you wrote it, and forgive me, your writing is almost as bad as mine, so could we perhaps just read out into the record the names of the people that you say that you saw in Ovcara. So I don't want to deal in any detail about these people, unless it's necessary, but I just want to go through the names so we've got them on the court record. So if you read them from your paper copy in front of you, it will be easier for you, I assure you. So who is the first person? Who is number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies for the handwriting, but believe me, when you're remembering these things it is very hard to keep your hand steady. Back to your question. Dragan Gavric. On my street, Dr. Mladen Stojanovic Street, a Croat that was next to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa Veber. His father is a hairdresser. My peer. That's three houses down the road from my shop. He's a Croat. Vlaho. I know he was an ambulance driver with the hospital, lived in the same house as the late Ljubisa Jurisic near the area known as two hills, or, rather, it was Tome Goreta [phoen] Street. He's a Croat, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 4, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Vidos, a hospital employee. His father was my manager, another Croat. At number 5 we see Pavlovic. I think his first name was Zeljko. Just across the way from my shop. A young man, aged about 24, a Croat. Number 6, Sinisa Glavasevic, a journalist, a Croat. Lili lived near the Catholic church. He was a Croat, a very proficient football player, but I can't remember his name. Number 8, Jurela, the son of Tomo and Zlata. Zlata used to work as a nurse at the hospital. He was a Croat, too. Zvonko Iles. When we were children, we used to call him Zriko. He's about my age, a Croat. Branko Polomija, a journalist, just like Sinisa Glavasevic. I don't know what his ethnic background was, but he was a rather young man. 11 and 12 are the Kolak brothers. They lived at Patkoviceva Street, Croats. I used to be friends with their father for long years. If only you could see their father and mother now. Oh, what a pitiful sight they are. They are like a couple of living dead; they can't seem to get over it. Herman Stjepan lived in the house next to my shop. The Kolak brothers were Croats, and Stjepan, too, was a Croat. The son of Car, the telephone operator. That's what you called him. Number 14, Herman, also known as Svabo. He came over from Germany at some point, even had a uniform. Number 15 is Ante Bodruzic. One of the managers at the Danube hotel, the head waiter. Rather young. I used to know him because I changed the upholstery on the furniture in one of his rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just stop you for a moment. Number 12 and number 13 -- well, it's really number 13 and number 14. Are you able to say what ethnicity they are, number 13 and number 14?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry for interrupting you. Let's move on to number 15. Are you able to say what ethnicity he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Bodruzic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let us resume then at number 16, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Kovac, a Croat, who used to work at the post office. To the very last day he was manning the phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 17, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragica Tuskan, and her son Drazen, Croats. Used to work with me for quite a long time, same company. Number 19, Markobasic. Can't remember the first name or ethnicity. I probably never even saw the lady until we were driven into Ovcara and then I saw a woman standing there across the way. Baumgertner; it's difficult to say anything about the ethnicity. The last name strikes me as German, but I really don't know what his stated ethnicity was. 21 was a man who came over from Nasice to help us out, almost as a tourist, you might say. Last name Kuhar. I remember him because he came to my warehouse. His shoe size was 48. Couldn't find a pair for him, unfortunately. He is still in Zagreb. Nobody wants to see him. He has no parents, and his brother refuses to go and get him because he was forfeit the compensation that the Croatian state has been paying him for missing persons. Now we get to Dado Djukic. His father was an X-ray technician. I have no idea what he might be in terms of ethnicity. Nikica Holjevac. Your Honours, he was a respectable, honourable man, just like you, and yet he was killed at Ovcara. Damir Polhert. He was the son of a good friend of mine. Because when I first started as an apprentice in upholstery, he was my master, as it were. And then Zeljko Begov, a Croat, who worked at the Nama department store, and he used to live right next door to the barracks. Number 26, Damjan Samardzic, as far as I heard, he was a truck driver. I never used to know him before, but I got to know him during the war. His stepson, Gaspar, that is to say, the son of his present wife. I don't know what the nationality is. Now number 28 and 29, they're both called Bosanac. One was almost 80 years old, and the other at the time must have been around my age, that is to say, 50 back then. And they lived close to the hospital. I think in the Bozidar Adzija Street, or as we used to call it Sapudl. Number 30 is Tomislav Bajdrauh, a friend of mine, my age, and yesterday I forgot to say maybe -- or did I mention it, Oliver Jovanovic. I think he was a Serb through his father, Djuro. And then Tomislav Pap who used to be a warehouse keeper at the hospital with Dr. Bosanac, and I don't know what his nationality was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I hear the word being interpreted as "nationality." I'm going to check in relation to ethnicity for number 26, et al. Can we just deal with number 26? I'm sorry to ask you this, but it hasn't come across terribly clearly. Let's go to 26, please. Do you know the ethnicity of number 26?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. No, no, I never used to know him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's all right. I'm not asking you to guess in any way. Number 27, 28, and 29, do you know the ethnicity of those people, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gaspar should be a Croat, judging by his surname, but I don't know for sure. And 29 and 28, as far as I can tell, I'm not sure, they're Croats because his son was courting my younger daughter. So that's how I know that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Finally this: How is it that you're able to remember 32 names and give a list of people that you say you saw at Ovcara 15 years after it happened? Can you tell the Court why you were able to remember these names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, it's quite simple. Those were people I used to see on a daily basis. I made the list of names the very next day, following my return from Sremska Mitrovica. I wrote down all of 27 names straight away, and just to jog my memory because women used to come to Plitvice Hotel and see me and ask me: Beli, did you see my husband? Did you see my boy? Or whatever. And so I could answer: Yes, I saw them at Ovcara. I don't know. I mean, this is no problem. I may have a problem with other things, such as fixing a broken TV set or something. But this is very easy. Those were neighbours of mine, so I have no problem remembering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Mr. Vasic, we will probably stop at about 20 past, so if you could keep that in mind. Because we're finishing earlier today, we'll shorten each session a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try and go through some technical points in the first part, and we won't be needing that much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berghofer. Let me introduce myself. I am Miroslav Vasic, one of the Defence counsels for Mr. Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have something I'd like to point out to you. So far you have been answering the questions by my colleague and you had to listen to translation. We are both speaking a language we both understand, so I would like to appeal to you to pause very briefly after my questions so that the interpretation can come through. First of all, let us go through some technical points in conjunction with the statements you made so far, and as far as I can see there's quite a bit. Since I do not know whether you've had the opportunity to consult the copies of your statements recently, I do have a bundle here. So I'd like to ask the usher to hand all these statements to you, and then you can give them back to us later. Mr. Berghofer, your first statement relating to the events in Vukovar in 1991, November 1991, dates back to the 6th of April in Zagreb. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Our colleagues from the Prosecution did provide us copies of your statements. I can't see, though, who this statement was given to. So could you tell me who it was on that day, on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, they came to collect me at Plitvice Motel, and I had to go to court. And that was the first statement I made, and I was asked to identify two men and tell what they did in Vukovar in the course of the war. Their family name was Dragosavac. Since those two were not the Dragosavac men who were considered to have done certain bad deeds in relation to Croats, and so I said: Gentlemen, the older one I do not know. And as far as I can remember, the younger one didn't say "boo" to anyone. And they approved it. They said: You're an honourable man. You only returned from Mitrovica three days ago, and you're an honest man. And as to Ovcara, some two people from MUP came to Motel Plitvice, as far as I can remember, and I dictated my statement to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Berghofer. Can you just tell me: You said that you dictated your statement to them. Did they show you a copy of that statement and did you sign it? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not sign it. It was in a notebook, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we just make sure. Could you be so kind and take a look. There should be a statement, a copy of a statement, in front of you. The title is "statement." And in the right-hand corner, it says VUBOR.421. And to the left it says "Dragutin Berghofer." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like you to tell me who you gave this statement to. Was this a statement you gave to the members of the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to start at the end because there have been some mistakes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see the date in the left corner, the 6th of April, 1992, on the last page? The bottom left corner.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say that 90 per cent of this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was not asking you about the contents of the statement; I was just asking whether this is the statement you gave to the MUP representatives.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Because there are certain names here, because some of the people who were with me didn't even know those boys. I was the only man who actually recognised Bulidza, who recognised Mugosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So far -- now you've had the opportunity to scan this text.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you the following: After that, you talked to the MUP representative of Croatia once again on the 1st of June, 1992, and there is official record of that. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I think I gave my statements as many as eight times so far. I can't remember every single one as such, but yes, I did give those statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. Could you maybe take a look at the document entitled "The Republic of Croatia, the Ministry of the Interior." And the date is the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Official record. Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It says that you were interviewed by Ivica Dodlek, an employee of the MUP. Did you talk to him and did he compile the report after that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now you've jogged my memory. That's this guy called Ivica. The thing is I couldn't quite remember earlier on, but that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then on the 16th and the 17th of June, 1995, you talked to the OTP from The Hague Tribunal, and on that occasion a statement was compiled which was read out to you in a language you could understand, and you signed it. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not read out to me, but I did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And prior to signing it, did you know what it contained? Were you sure that it contained exactly what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I can't argue with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After making a statement to the OTP, you were interviewed as a witness before the investigating magistrate of the municipal court at Vinkovci on the 7th of March, 1996 in a criminal case. Is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. This was a case against the defendants at the time, Veljko Kadijevic, et al., and in that case did you give testimony before the investigating magistrate at the municipal court in Vinkovci in 1996? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against Kadijevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That man had nothing to do with me. I have no idea about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you just take a look in front of you. In this stack of documents there should be one entitled "Record of Witness Statement," and it says KIO741/95-52, and it says "Dragutin Berghofer, Witness," and the criminal case against Veljko Kadijevic, et al. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I can't remember that. Perhaps it was the cooperative of the former camp inmates from Vukovar, and they lodged a complaint. They actually sued Mr. Kadijevic as a cooperative. I can't remember having said anything about Kadijevic in particular myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you just take a look on the first page, by the end of the page to the right there's a signature, in the right corner -- in the bottom corner of every page. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So it is indeed possible that you made this statement to the investigating magistrate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be, but I can't remember blaming -- I did blame the JNA, and I did it together with my fellow inmates, if that's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No. I didn't say that you gave evidence directly against Veljko Kadijevic; I'm just saying that you made a statement in this case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Shortly afterwards, following a request from my learned friends from the OTP you came to The Hague and you gave evidence in a case according to Rule 61 before this Tribunal. It was on the 27th of March, 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that you appeared before the Trial Chamber as a witness in a court case before this Tribunal, and it was on the 4th of February, 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Prior to that testimony, did you receive copies of your statements from my OTP colleagues, the statements that you made to the OTP investigators? Did you read them? And were you asked whether you had any remarks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did read through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this day, on the 26th of April, 2004, you again gave evidence following a request from the district court for war crimes in Belgrade, and you gave your statement before the court in Zagreb. And you made a statement and you signed it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Finally, you also gave evidence before the district court for war crimes in Belgrade during two days, on the 25th and the 26th of October, 2004, and there is a transcript of that testimony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: In the course of all of these testimonies, you've always tried to make statements according to the best of your recollection because you have always been warned of the need to tell the truth and the consequences of perjury. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I have finished with the technical bit, and I think that this would be a suitable time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I would like to get on with my questions now. Up until the 24th of October, 1991, you were living in your own house at Sajmiste. How far was that from the barracks, the JNA barracks, in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight or nine metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You later moved to a different house where you say you stayed until the 17th of November, 1991. How far was that house from the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This other house -- well, you have the barracks, you have the Slavija mill -- well, say about 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a member of Vukovar's 204th Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was only recognised later on, but, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We're familiar with the problems surrounding the recognition of that particular brigade. Once the war had ended, you were not exactly happy with your own status, the status you were later to be granted as a member of the Vukovar Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite how it was. I was quite happy. Where does the problem seem to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Didn't you believe that some people were granted recognitions and awards which they had not earned during the fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite true. One thing I was unhappy about was that I had had five houses and two shops before the war, and all my country gave me afterwards was a small 35 -- was a small flat of 35 square metres, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, when exactly did you join the preparations for the armed struggle? Was that as early as May 1991, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one thing I can tell you is that I was never into politics, and I was not in favour of any subversive activity against the previous country. I had put an enormous effort into building the house that I had, and once they tore that house down the tide turned for me, and I was no longer in favour of the JNA. Yet everybody was still saying: There will be a truce, there will be a truce, so day by day I kept deciding to stay in Vukovar and not leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What you've just told us is in reference to August 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about between the 5th and the 8th of August, 1991? Were you involved in any preparations for armed combat in the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us, the people of Vukovar, or nearly all of us, although we were not all directly involved, the official date is the 2nd of May for all of us. However, at certain points I was on duty at the local commune building, at the radio station, Nikola Papac and myself, Marko Oric, those people. We were on duty there, although it was a perfectly regular occurrence that people still chose to stay in Vukovar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me who was in charge of all these duty shifts and securing certain house and streets. Who organised this entire thing at the level of the entire town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a very professional set-up. Nikola Papac just asked me whether I would keep him company. What are you doing tonight, he said. And he said: The MUP people told me should there be an incident in one of the villages around Vukovar that I should go and report to them. So I just decided to join him. We were very good friends, and I decided to keep him company for the night at the local commune building in Stjepan Radica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about the fact that you were a member of the 204th Brigade. As far as I know, it was only established sometime in September 1991, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I remember. It wasn't before I was a detainee in Sremska Mitrovica that the 104th and the 204th Brigades first came into existence. But I don't think it was that early on. Don't take my word for it, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There was something else I wanted to ask you about this. Wasn't it the National Guards Corps that you joined at first?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, did I get your name right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The National Guards Corps, I was a grandfather by this time with three grandchildren, and I was pushing 51. I don't think your question is appropriate; that is at least what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. But the reason I ask this is because that's what your statement indicates, the statement that you gave to the Vinkovci investigating magistrate on the 7th of March, 1996, on page 2 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friend, the English reference is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember telling them that you had joined the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If those civilians were National Guards Corps members, then I have no choice but to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please go to page 2 of the statement, in case you found it. The statement is dated the 7th of March, 1996. A statement to the investigating magistrate, record of witness interview. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: 7th of March, 1996. You have witness information on the title page, and that might be easier for you to track down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the date anywhere. Is that what it says in English up here?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, no. The heading should be "Record of Witness Interview." That's what it says in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. I can't find my way around all these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll have the usher assist you. I have a copy of this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This says "Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's not Zagreb; it's Vinkovci. Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go to page 2 of this document. Paragraph 4 begins with the word "immediately." Can you please read that aloud, the first two sentences.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. "Immediately after the occupation of Vukovar, out of all of the units that I mentioned, I joined the ZNG and Vukovar's defence. We resisted the attacks until the 18th of November." Should I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No need, thank you. Do you remember stating this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that I did. There were many such statements. You see the pile of documents in front of me, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were a member of the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion of the 204th Vukovar Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Menges came along and said that, didn't he.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this brigade have a number of units at Mitnica, Sajmiste, Borovo, Priljevo and in the surroundings of the hospital? Were all those units part of the 204th Vukovar Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see where you're going with this question, and I can only confirm that Vukovar's defenders were in those areas, too. I didn't go there to see them, but I'm sure that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that. Thank you. Can you tell us how many battalions the brigade comprised? You, yourself, for part of the 1st Battalion. Did you know at the time or did you later on find out how many battalions the brigade comprised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hardly be expected to know that, Mr. Vasic. We were a very, very small group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the 1st Battalion positioned exactly in August 1991 and later on in November 1991? So August and November, that's what I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were 200 metres from the fence surrounding the barracks. There's an orchard that I owned in the vicinity, so I know the area. The area is usually referred to as Slavija. It's a small area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did they hold on to these positions into November 1991 or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 17th, is that what your question is about, which date was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, you can tell us which day it was when the defenders left those positions.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 17th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many companies your battalion comprised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Vasic. I was a warehouse keeper.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your capacity as a warehouse keeper, did you provide any supplies for your battalion or perhaps for the brigade or perhaps for the residents of Vukovar or the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did take supplies to the hospital two or three times. We took some sugar for Dr. Vesna Bosanac. Nikola Papac was still alive. We brought some coffee, too. As far as I know, that was it for the hospital. On the last day only, just before the army got there - and we may discuss that later on - as for the other brigades, they never got any supplies from us because we, ourselves, were not too strong on supplies. We had about 2.000 civilians to look after. That's a ballpark figure. I'm sure you understand. The street is full of cellars, because there is hillside just behind the houses stretching about 20 metres away from the houses. As for those positions over there, as far as I remember, there were at least between 80 and 90 people manning those positions, give or take a man or two, people that it was my duty to look after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you went about your duties, did you ever meet anyone called Franjo Kracak at the positions near Sajmiste?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did meet him. I knew him before the war, too, but he was younger than I was, and we hardly ever exchanged greetings. He was wearing a uniform, I do remember that, and I gave him two or three chocolate bars that I got from the warehouse. And I never saw him again. But I did know him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say you knew him. Can you tell us if he was a mortar expert.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Vasic. But if I can help, his nickname was Brada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who was in command of your company, the 2nd Company of the 1st Battalion, during the fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me a minute, I may be able to explain what I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was, in Stjepan Radica Street there was a local board building a local commune building that had been demolished by shelling. We moved to the so-called Hungarian street. It's further down Radiceva Street. People from Vukovar know that. The building currently houses the police administration, so that was where we moved to. And believe it or not, there were seven or eight of us who owned private businesses. We joined forces, put together a bit of money, and organised a defence for Vukovar for the small area that I described as Slavija, near the barracks. None of us were schooled officers or anything like that. The first commander there was Tomislav Berendi who was a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you just repeat this person's last name, and I didn't hear it clearly enough myself, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first commander at the local commune building in Stjepan Radica Street was Tomislav Berendi, a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that during August, before the fighting broke out in Vukovar, there was a check-point at Sajmiste where people leaving Vukovar for Negoslavci were stopped, as well as those driving back into Vukovar. Do you know if there was one to begin with, and do you know that it had been organised by the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really confirm that, but I know that people were talking about something that sounds very much like this. I wasn't there myself, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if a part of your unit was positioned at the Stjepan Supanc school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I was wondering if you could help us out with this. If we considered the defence line in Vukovar, what does the term "Osa 3" mean, O-s-a 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. Vasic, and anything I know I am willing to share with you. First you had Vuka 1, Vuka 2, and Vuka 3. And then Josip Tomasic was stung by a wasp, so then it was no longer Vuka 1, Vuka 2, Vuka 3. Now it became Osa 1, Osa 2, Osa 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, "Osa" means wasp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these defence lines that were called this in certain places?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were check-points set-up at a number of private homes, some sort of a guard, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Ivica Pancic mean anything to you? Did it mean anything to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the time and not now. I really don't know, but I think he was a rather young man. It was not entirely strange that I didn't know him or notice him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We could perhaps show you the same map that you were shown by my learned friend, the map of Vukovar. Could you use it to mark the defence lines held by your battalion.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, as far as I know, you, too, grew up in Yugoslavia. Do you know what a battalion means? As far as I know, that's a whole lot of soldiers, isn't it? Do you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I definitely do, Mr. Berghofer. I definitely do. But can you at least mark the positions held by members of your company, if you can; if not, please just say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure I can, sure. No problem at all. I can tell you about it without looking at the map. Pavkovic, Mikara [phoen], the small area also known as Slavija --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 156 run up on the screen, please. As soon as we have it, I would like to have it enlarged and the witness can tell us when it's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's in as far as I'm able at all to find my way around the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have the central portion of the map enlarged, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this enough for you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please hand the witness the pen that was previously used to make markings?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark the positions of your company, the ones you held on to until the 17th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this long line you can see right here, is that the road to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The line running down the middle of the map is the road to Negoslavci, and there's another line to the lower right corner. That's the road to Sotin.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sotin and on to Belgrade. And what about this thing here on the right-hand side? Is that the water-tower by any chance? Right here where it reads "JNA" and then somewhere down from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It says JNA --

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there is an arrow to the left from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is Mitnica. And the water-tower I do not think is marked on this actual map.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if I could find the water-tower I could just turn from there, and the distance is about 200 metres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But please try to use the barracks as your reference point.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how can I if we have this line running down the middle of the map? But it should be around here at any rate. Just a minute, please. I don't want to go wrong on this, because, after all, I live there. But let's say it might be around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you now please draw a line to mark the position of the defence line, and mark it with a number 1, and then circle it, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's this line right here where the arrow touches down near this street?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think these are the streets of Vukovar, and the small squares you can see there are actually houses.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's a street, then it must be Mladena Stojanovica Street, if my understanding is correct. That's how it should be. The barracks is right here. Let's try to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I assume the defence lines ran along certain streets. Can you draw a line to indicate where the defence lines were.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, they were stationed at Patkoviceva Street, which is right next to Mladena Stojanovica Street. And you have Mladena Stojanovica Street right there, and there's a sports hall right there. I'm not sure if you know. It should be somewhere around these parts. It's all a bit of a jumble here on this map, but the whole thing was about 300 metres from the barracks itself. The distance was no greater than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you've marked two positions for us, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: One's just off the barracks and the other one is at Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not at Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The water-tower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, closer to the town's centre. We had nothing to do with Mitnica, where the sports hall is, if you can find it. It's up on a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark this spot on the right-hand side with a number 1 and circle it, please, and the other one in front of the barracks with a number 2 and circle it, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just stress, micro area Slavija is up there on the hill bordering on the street of Dr. Mladen Stojanovic Patkoviceva Street, just so as to avoid any misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like for this map to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 230.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We won't be needing this picture anymore for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. You, as member of this unit, also had an automatic rifle. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not have one, no. A fortnight before the fall, I received a gun and during the breakthrough I exchanged it for an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So it was only during the breakthrough that you were carrying that automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I exchanged it right in front of the forest, and I gave my gun in exchange for an automatic rifle, and I then returned it afterwards. When we came to the hospital, I placed it under a burnt car next to the barracks and next to the hospital, and not a single bullet had been fired from that weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I am understanding you correctly, what you're saying is that this rifle and the ammunition was placed under this car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there was no ammunition, there was just an automatic rifle. And as to whether there was any ammunition actually in the rifle, believe me, and you will have to believe me, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I do believe you. Thank you. Can you just tell me with reference to this shed, is it within the parameter of the hospital, close to the casualty?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's where it has always been.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether any other members of your company had hand-held grenades, apart from automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This is too much to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me whether at any point by the end of October/beginning of November, a general mobilisation, call for mobilisation, took place in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't help you on that one. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, do you know which Vukovar defence units were stationed around the Count Eltz's castle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't believe there were any units in that area. As far as I know, there was nothing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And have you ever heard about the units under the command of Mr. Stjepan Radas was deployed there at any given time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the Radas I have in mind, if that's the one, that is, I only met him at some point in 1994. But I really don't know about that. The one I mean was a youngish man. I was 52, 53 at the time, and he might have been around 40, if that's the man you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He was one of the commanders who was a former JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. Vasic. These people were far out of my range.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. What were your tasks in relation to logistics? What did you have to do and how did you find out about the needs of individual units?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I had to do nothing. I just told you that we as private citizens got organised without anyone's assistance, and we even bought an ox from a Serb because the JNA plane had bombed his farm. And so his stables were on fire and he had no money left, and so he came to see me and he said to me: Beli, I don't have enough money to pay for my father's funeral, but I have an ox that I'd like to buy [as interpreted], and so we got together. I can tell you how many private citizens did that. And we gave him money to pay for his father's funeral. And we took the ox, and we provided food for both the civilians and those lads up there, about 70 to 80 of them. But let me continue by telling you that we would get a couple of hams or pieces of bacon from Djakovo for as long as you could travel through. But water was the biggest problem, in fact, because all the wells had already been destroyed, and there was no municipal water supply. There hadn't been any for a long time at that stage. And we had no yeast, you know. I suppose you understand what I mean. So we couldn't bake proper bread, and perhaps we'll come to that bit later, when I saw bread for the first time after two and a half months. So that's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now about wells, were the wells down in the area of Sajmiste as well? Is that the area you're referring to, or did you know about the wells in all of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have an insight into all of Vukovar. What I'm telling you about is the Stjepana Radica Street which is the main road leading to Sotin and Belgrade and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the course of the war, did you ever see HOS members in the area of Sajmiste and thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, at that stage there were no formations when allegedly the HOS people were there, whether they were there before us, but I can tell you that I saw only three people wearing uniforms at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that the others were civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the people who were with me, yes, and the furthest I got to was Slavija and the hospital, roughly speaking, 400 metres away, three bus stops away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned you went to the hospital. I imagine that you met your friend Mr. Ivankovic there, you mentioned you were friends with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, I took a tooth-brush to Dr. Kolak because she was unable to go back home. And so she said to me: Yes, please, Beli, find me a tooth-brush, even a second-rate one. And she was a dentist, and of course she was annoyed that she couldn't brush her teeth. And obviously I met Dr. Ivankovic as well, and he couldn't go home because he had no trousers. And so I gave him a pair of trousers and a pair of shoes and a jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you ever heard Dr. Ivankovic complain about the fact that he was uncomfortable because the hospital Crisis Staff were not treating him nicely?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only found about that for the first time five years later when I first saw him after the liberation, that is to say, after Vukovar was joined with the -- to the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us about this breakthrough that you started on the 17th of November, 1991. Can you tell me where this decision was made, where were you when the decision was made.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in the offices of the now-local community -- I mean, the Hungarian school down there in the Radica Street. And Osa made the decision: Okay, let's go for the breakthrough. And we said: Okay, let's go, because the shelling was so intense back then. I can't explain this to you. It was horrible. And so we went for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me approximately how many people set off. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. I can see it clearly in my mind's eye even now. I mean, I was heading the column because I grew up in that area in the suburb around the hospital, next to the police station, the municipal building, and there is a cemetery there which has been disused for a long time. And if you are even faintly familiar with Vukovar, the end of the column reached the Lola Ribar Street next to the Autobacka offices. And then we went in the direction of the police station, and so we were all in a column. And then we turned left toward the prison used to be. And then we crossed Bozidar Adzija Street.
