We turned right in the direction of the cemetery, and we crossed the cemetery. We crossed a football stadium, the football club was called Sloga, and we crossed the grounds of that football stadium. And we came out -- and I'm trying to remember the name of the street. Well, never mind. It was the main street leading to Adica, and then we came to the railway line. And -- yeah, Borisa Kidrica Street. And there was a carriage standing in the middle of the road, and there was so many of us that you could hear the sound of our feet. And two metres further up there is a railway bridge. When they heard us, I don't know whether it was the JNA or who it was, don't misunderstand me, I don't know, but they were shelling us so much they felt the sound of our feet. And there were about 350 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just two more points on what you've just said. You said there were JNA people or who it was. Who else did you mean? Did you mean the TO, Vukovar, the locals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't think of them straight away because locals did not have any airplanes, any tanks, or any mortars, Mr. Vasic. Can you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I do agree, but I'm talking about this event.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. On this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But there were no tanks or planes there. Can you tell me about this column. How long could it have been, if you could give me a rough assessment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 200 metres, a winding column. I was heading the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As long as the decision was made, the breakthrough decision, you started off straight away?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of the town hall, and the TO offices - what should I say? - the military offices, just to make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the defence Crisis Staff there at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at a certain point, but when we got there we found nobody there, empty rooms. I have to tell you this as well: Myself and Bili -- well, there was a teleprinter there, and he said: Do you know how to use it? And I said: Well, I'm useless at any of this. And he started -- and he said: There's no way out. And we found no one. Everything was deserted. Okay, yes, we did find Branko Borkovic. And then we went on to the town hall and it was all dark. There was no electricity. And we started debating. And at around 10.30 p.m., one group set off and then the other group that I was leading. And when we arrived at the railroad track at the corner of the Sloga football stadium and the forest, it was just horrible. And the people who were crossing the Vuka River in front of me, two people were blown into the air, blown to pieces, and some people thought it was me. And Beli was said to be dead in Zagreb. And actually I turned back and I returned to the garage together with Njofra Jankovic, Marko Mandic, his wife, and this doctor, Dr. Aleksijevic, I think he was an orthopaedic surgeon, and his wife as well. And Njofra Jankovic, yes, I've mentioned him already, and we turned back and returned to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just clarify this: You said you came across Bili there. Is it Marin Vidic, Bili, that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, on your way back, and you said which route you took, did you go straight to the hospital, you never stopped anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And why did you go in the direction of the hospital, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the entire town was moving in that direction. One square metre of the hospital grounds had at least three people standing and four beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was it the Crisis Staff decision that those people who didn't want to go for the breakthrough to withdraw within the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had nothing to do with it. It was just that Osa said: In case anyone is wounded, we won't go back for him. It was an amateur effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you talked about the column. Was it the members of your company or the battalion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were from our company, and God knows where all those people had come from. It was night-time. We didn't have that many people on our positions. At the Slavija micro area that I supplied, I don't know. We didn't even know that so many people had remained in Vukovar. When they all descended upon the hospital, it was an enormous crowd of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me: Where did you hear for the first time that Mrs. Vesna Bosanac said that those who came to the hospital wearing uniforms should throw away their uniforms and discard their weapons and change into civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no uniform. I had my own civilian clothes, and let me just stress: I didn't even have any buttons on my clothes. That didn’t mean anything to me, if she had ordered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you see anyone else discarding their uniforms and putting on civilian clothes and discarding weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw them taking off yellow shoes, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see it on the 17th, when you got to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw that on the 19th, in the afternoon -- no, no, no. On the 18th -- we are talking about the 17th, yes, it was on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether at that time you saw a great many defenders of Vukovar arriving at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Mr. Vasic, but I saw very many people wounded, very many of them indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the investigating magistrate in Vinkovci that apart from the medical staff and the wounded, you also saw 2.000 civilians at the hospital and quite a few defenders of the city of Vukovar amongst them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case you have read this, I believe you that I could have said that, and it is indeed true. I told you that earlier on that quite a few civilians -- I mean, I'm telling you I don't know where all these people had come from. And certainly amongst those young men there must have been defenders of Vukovar, I'm not arguing with that, but I wasn't with them. I knew people from my own age, from my own group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you see any of the people who arrived at the hospital on those days and had participated in the defence of Vukovar, either as members of military formations or as MUP members? Did you see them placing bandages on themselves or wearing plaster-casts, even though they were not wounded. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that, because about five days before the fall of Vukovar there was no way you could drive anywhere by car because everything was blocked up. And I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't see any of the fighters from your own company who wasn't wounded but was wearing a plaster-cast or a bandage at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that some of the defenders of Vukovar put on white coats in order to appear to be medical staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I saw Damjan Samardzic; he was wearing a white coat. But for a while he did actually work at the hospital. He was a warehouse keeper for at least a month and a half. He worked at the hospital, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he one of the commanders of the ZNG units in Vukovar; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to help you. He was nicknamed big Bojler. Let's suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that Mr. Kolesar was wearing a white coat as well? Did you see him wearing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Kolesar is Vukovar person, and some people might be amazed that I'm remembering all these names, but I used to meet them on a daily basis. Kolesar was not wearing a white coat. Kolesar is a Ruthenian by ethnicity and Licina was a Serb, and Hetak Salajdzija [phoen], according to his family name I believe was a Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. That's why I'm asking these questions of you because you know people in Vukovar. Can you tell me whether you saw a person called Bozidar Segec at the hospital, if you know him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the Segec I'm thinking of, three houses down the road there are three Segec men, father and two sons, and there was another Segec who I think back then was 25 years younger than me. But now that you have mentioned it, I'm remembering what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to know: Are you aware of the fact that he was a member of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know a person called Milan Mlinaric?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know Perica Mlinaric from Borovo, but I don't know about this other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Zelimir Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And Dragutin Friscic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tomislav Lesic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Zdenko Novak?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we move into private session for a moment because of a couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us about arriving at the hospital. You weren't sick or wounded yourself, were you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How come you remained in the hospital if you were neither? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, there was nowhere else for me to go. It was dark. I was terrified. It was raining, and it was a wasteland all around. And after all, there were about 2.000 people there, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Dr. Ivankovic allowed you to stay in the hospital until the morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He saw me on the 19th at about 1.00 and said: What are you doing here of all people? And I said: Well, I've been here since the night of the 17th. And he said: Come with me. So there we were. Perkovic and I were sitting in one of his offices in the hospital. It was a windowless office or room. There were some nurses there, too, as far as I remember, as well as Dr. Aleksijevic and his wife. There were about ten of us sitting in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The idea of the Defence teams was to divide our questions up among ourselves, and my learned friends will be asking you other things about this. But I'll move on to the point when you claim you arrived at Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prior to which, Your Honour, I would like some instructions from you, please. We have a different regime today, and when do we take our next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It could be as early as now, Mr. Vasic, because we would be finishing at about 1.15, so if we broke now it could be a convenient division of time. You seem to have reached a point where that would be a practical arrangement. Is that so? Well, perhaps then --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- we'll give the witness an opportunity to have a break now, and we will resume at a quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I'd like to ask you something about your testimony in relation to Ovcara. You say that on the 20th of November, 1991, at about 1330 hours you arrived at Ovcara in buses, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The buses you arrived on, were they driving in a column, one after the other?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the ones at the rear. I know about the ones at the head of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that your bus was the fourth from the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I remember that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you were kept waiting for about ten minutes until the first three buses in front of you were emptied. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answer to a question by my learned friend, you tried to add up the people you remembered who got into the hangar and you arrived at a total of between 140 and 160. Does that mean that all these people entered the hangar within those ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, when I got off the bus, I took the rear entrance or the rear door to be inspected by Mugosa. I was being beaten and being searched, so that's how long it took for the people to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How much time would you say? Plus the ten minutes you spent waiting on the bus, how long did the search take and you running the gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, everything I saw from the bus was in those ten minutes. Later on it was done with. I went to see Mugosa. He went through my pockets, searched me, and I crossed the seven or eight metres to reach the gauntlet. I was beaten and other people were being beaten, too. So there you have it, a total of perhaps 15 minutes, give or take a minute or two. I don't need to be more specific than this. I guess you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means I do. But just to sum it up, the whole thing took 15 minutes between your arrival at Ovcara and the time you got into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were on the bus and then you got off the bus. Did you see many people outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the young soldiers there who headed left. I saw Karlovic, Vili Karlovic, who was with me on the bus. There were people there in addition to those who were beating other people, there were about a dozen to the them to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said about ten people or a dozen in addition to those who were doing the beating. In answer to my learned friend's question, you said that those beating the other people were also about ten men, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the same applies to the situation inside the hangar, the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I free to conclude three times ten would roughly amount to about 30 people altogether, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- well, 25, 30. The beating was severe. You just try to get through the gauntlet as quickly as you could in order to take refuge inside. See my point?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There's one matter I need to clarify. You used the term "reservists" in answer to a question by my learned friend. Can we agree that when saying that when using that term you did not in any way include those serving their regular military term with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Or -- and likewise, you do not take that term to include JNA officers, regular officers, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been some of those among them, too, but it was really difficult to tell them. I'm giving you an honest account. They were just dressed the way they were, and you didn't have time to look them in the eyes or anything. If it had been you wearing that sort of uniform at the time, I would not have been able to tell you from Adam. Do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm talking about the reservists. When you said the reservists, did you mean the paramilitaries, the members of the various paramilitary groups that you spoke about as well as locals wearing olive-drab uniforms? I suppose all of us who did our regular military term with the JNA had one of those at one time or other.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question. In the previous army, when you've completed your military term, you either get a rank or you can get an assignment with the reserve forces. For example, Zeljko Mojko [phoen] at Modateks, when he came for Dudas was displaying the rank of captain, but this was the only rank that I was able to identify among those people. As for the rest, I can't really say who they belonged to, but they were somewhat different from the local paramilitaries. That much I did notice. There were three different kinds of uniform: The young, the reservists, and the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Those you term the reservists, did you recognise among those people quite a number of those who were locals, who were from the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this man who drove us to Mitnica; he shook hands with me. He used to see me at the chemist that I owned and the upholstery business. His wife worked with the town's land surveyor's office, but I don't know his name. Djuro, he drove us to Mitnica, was wearing plain clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, a Vukovar Territorial Defence detachment or the Petrova Gora Territorial Defence detachment? I mean once you returned to Croatia after your captivity.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Vukovar one, and I heard about the TO near the municipality building. Can't say I didn't because I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know the members of these units, these Serbian TO people, were wearing precisely the sort of uniform that you described the reservists wearing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but their uniforms struck me as a little older for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you entered the hangar, were people being lined up in some sort of order or did they just stand wherever they wanted to? You've described your own position to us, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. People just rushed into the hangar, which is lightning quick, if you know what I mean. Some people were struck down and some of them managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that. I'm waiting for the interpretation. Can you tell us, sir, once you were inside the hangar, Mr. Cakalic got in, and what about Mr. Guncevic, do you remember seeing him there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I had not known Guncevic prior to this time; it was only at Mitrovica that I learned his name. And he was with me in Mitrovica. Other than that, I hadn't even recognised him in the hangar. As for Cakalic, we go back a long way, 40 years at least. I rushed left on the way into the hangar and headed for the far end of the hall. And those at the back were beating and kicking people, and when my turn came I tried to go more towards the middle of the crowd, and Cakalic was right there, standing about three metres to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief about the beating of Mr. Damir Samardzic, also known as Veliki Bojler and his relative Gaspar. Where were you when that occurred? Just tell us about your whereabouts because you told us about the rest yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still on the bus. He was seated right in front of me on the same bus. He went out the front door. And Goran Vidas was on the bus, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this, because now I'm about to ask you something else. There's a photograph that I would like to show you, and if you could please mark this spot where you saw these people being beaten as you were watching from the bus and when some of them fell down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ERN number, Your Honours, is 00531231. This is photograph -- number 22, rather, page number 22. Could you blow this up for us, please, or rather zoom in so we can see the door to the hangar in the middle of the image. Will you please zoom in a bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this all right for you, Mr. Berghofer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the usher please hand the witness a pen so that he can mark the spot for us, the spot where he saw Damjan Samardzic and his relative being beaten as he was watching from the bus and they remained on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please place a cross to mark the spot where they were beaten and put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is there sufficient space -- sufficient room for you to mark where they remained lying on the ground with a 2 and a 3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same place, roughly speaking. Off to the right there was a ditch. You know what a ditch is, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A water ditch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a small cross where the ditch was and put a number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir. Now that we have the photograph up, can you please mark the position where you and the other persons were standing who were taken out of the hangar at one point waiting to be taken back to Vukovar and put a number 3 there, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just a small cross and a number 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek that this be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 231.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a proposal to make. We might be needing this in the future, so we might want a blank photograph also to be admitted into evidence because we are likely to be using it with some future witnesses, to have a blank copy ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It can come up on the screen quickly, Mr. Vasic. Is that sufficient for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. If it's quickly retrievable, there is no reason for it to be tendered as a separate exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll no longer be using this. Thank you, Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you say you saw Mr. Cakalic on his way into the hangar or once he had entered. You didn't see him being beaten outside, but you did see him being beaten inside the hangar. Do you remember what he looked like after he had received the beating, when you saw him inside the hangar, or even perhaps when you saw him later on outside the hangar as you were standing there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was bruised on the right side of his body and he had been beaten on his back. That's what he complained about, at least. But nothing that particularly triggers any memories.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does he aware glasses normally; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, he does, but not necessarily when he's just walking the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the time you saw him inside the hangar? Was he wearing glasses or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief about young Baumgertner and Kemo, who was the man beating him, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that while testifying in another case before this Tribunal, the Dokmanovic case, you actually said you weren't sure that the person was young Baumgertner. You weren't sure then or at the time of testifying. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct, Mr. Vasic. I'm still not absolutely positive about the person's identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say you saw Slavko Dokmanovic inside the hangar at one point in time. Can you remember the exact time, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, the last time I testified - and you've got to take my word for it - my brain was just stuck for the exact time. I couldn't for the life of me remember whether it was 1330 hours or what time it was. And believe me, I did actually look at the watch at the time. It was 1330 hours, 1.30 p.m., the sun was high in the sky. It was a beautiful day. By the time they had unloaded all of us, well, Dokmanovic might have been there between 1400 hours and 1430 hours. That's as specific as I can be based on pure memory. I wasn't exactly checking my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that. It's very difficult to be more specific than that, especially under the circumstances. I wanted to have from you a very general idea when he might have been there. Sir, are you certain that the man you saw there between 1400 hours and 1430 hours was Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely positive, 200 per cent, if you like. He was the municipal president, after all. I could not have mistaken him for anybody else. He had something that looked very much like an aviator's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm asking is there's information indicating that Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic was in fact at a government meeting at the same time you claim that he was at Ovcara. That's why I'm asking if you're positive.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Positive, Mr. Vasic. I'm absolutely positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that after Slavko Dokmanovic left you didn't see him again, that you saw a reservist coming into the hangar with a whistle. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that reservist a local? Was he from the area of Vukovar? Did you maybe know who he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember him, and I didn't know him, and I didn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he wearing the old uniform, the old reservist uniform that you referred to when you talked about the TO of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this reservist with a whistle came in, you were taken out of the hangar, is that true, and that was before the beatings in the hangar started. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vasic. There were beatings, followed by more beatings, and there were whistles, and one group was coming -- was coming out and the other was coming in. And it went on for about an hour and a half, this relentless beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But you heard the beatings, you heard the cries and screams, and you didn't see it. You came out of the hangar before it started?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Vasic. You have been misinformed. I saw it. I was an eye-witness. People were beaten up in front of my very -- before my very eyes. And then it continued after I left, so I heard the screams afterwards. But before I went out of the hangar, I could see it and I could hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you make a different statement to Mr. Ivan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the second name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: -- An employee of the MUP in Croatia when you talked to him on the 21st of June, 1992? Did you tell him that you were taken out of the hangar before the beatings started?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, Berghofer can never forget this, and I'm never going to make a mistake about this. You may rest assured that Berghofer, that is to say myself, has never made a mistake about this at all. I told you, even before, we were beaten up even as we were -- this man would come in with a whistle and then he would say: That's enough. And one group would go out, and I said to myself: Thank God. But then the next group was in in no time. And it was just more of the same, and also later when I went out I heard had that the beatings were still going on and the people were still moaning and screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained all that. What you have in front of you is a document entitled "Official Report." Can you find it? It is dated the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is on page 035 in the B/C/S version, 71460, and it's actually page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the sake of my learned friend, in the English version it is 00578275, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you be so kind, Mr. Berghofer, and look at the paragraph starting with "on the same day."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you on page 2 or on page 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On page 3. So halfway through the page, a paragraph starting "on the same day." Just below the reference to the Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's what it is, "Official Report." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. So this is the first page where it says "Official Report," and then another page, and then it's on the next page, on page number 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: So page number 3, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Halfway down the page the words "on the same day."

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you read it through and the sentence that follows as well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the same day at around 5.30 the reservist entered the hangar once again and he indicated by blowing a whistle that the most brutal physical abuse and mistreatment should start."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the next phrase, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Before the start of this abuse, Goran Ivankovic came along and separated me from the rest."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember stating this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it wasn't at 5.30; it was at 3.30. I'm not the only one saying that. If you have any other witnesses from Ovcara -- I will tell you, as we were leaving Ovcara it was getting a little bit darker and a car with the headlights on was driving in the opposite direction. Do you agree that there may have been a mistake in the note-taking or the translation or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly. So what you are arguing about is the time and not the content? You are saying that it's 3.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just before the matter proceeds, I've got the document. I don't accuse my learned friend of misquoting in any way at all. But as far as I can see, from a typed copy there is no signature from Mr. Berghofer, indicating that this is his statement. It is a report. Is that right or not? Because before my learned friend tries to tie down the witness, surely in fairness he should be asked whether he saw the contents of this statement, whether he agreed the statement, and whether in actual fact it's accurate and accords with his recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is precisely for this reason that at the start of my cross-examination I talked to the witness about all the statements or the documents that he had signed and that other people had signed on the basis of what he had said, and it was all in his presence. I have no intention of misleading or confusing the witness in any way. I've shown all these statements to him at the very start of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, all I'm saying, quite simply, is if it is Mr. Berghofer's statement, could my learned friend please refer me to where the signature is supposed to be, because I've looked at both the typed copy and the original and I can't find any signature whatsoever. Now, I don't deny my learned friend can cross-examine, but he has to have a correct basis for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not the effect of the earlier evidence, Mr. Vasic, that this may have been somebody's compilation from what was said rather than an actual statement of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't tell the witness that this was his statement. I just said that it was an official report from the MUP employee that he had talked to, and this record has been made on the basis of that interview, and I don't suppose the witness is confused in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you shouldn't rely on the witness remembering back to your questions before the break on that, just so that this is clear that this is not an actual signed statement of the witness, and then your questioning can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, we'll have to dwell on this statement a little bit longer. Is this statement that I asked you about -- or rather, this official record, what Ivan Dodaj [as interpreted], a MUP employee, wrote down after your account of the events following his official meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Dodaj may well be his name, but I'm telling you: You know that as early as the 20th of November at 4.00, it is already dark and I stressed in all my statements -- let's forget about this Dodaj. I really have no idea who he is. But I never made this mistake because otherwise it would have been at night-time that we had left Ovcara. We left when there was still day-light, and darkness was beginning to fall and another car was driving from the opposite direction and the lights were already on. And I said over and over again that we spent about two hours at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. All I was asking you about was whether you did indeed talk to this person and whether this text that you did not sign, you recognise your own words. Maybe he made a mistake about the time. What I want to know is whether you remember the fact that you gave a statement to this official at the time when he indicates this in his report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, what follows is incorrect as well, because some Dodaj can't go misrepresenting my memory of the events and about the beatings, et cetera. It is not correct. It just does not tally with the way these events actually took place. First of all, there was these horrible beatings. People were being massacred, and then Ivankovic came along after that, Goran Ivankovic. Let me just stress once again: Bulidza was not there at the time, the guy from the municipality, the president, Dokmanovic, was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. All I'm interested in is one thing: Did you have this interview with this MUP employee and did he record your words wrongly? I would just like to know whether you did talk to him, but obviously you didn't sign the statement, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, this was on the 1st of June, 1992. Some guys came along to Hotel Plitvice -- but believe me, I really don't remember this. And also you must believe me that I can't go wrong on that. Such horrific events remain etched in your mind forever, and I do remember that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to dwell on this document any longer. Can you tell me: When were you taken out of the hangar, at what time approximately?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 3.30, about 20 minutes -- 25 minutes that we spent waiting outside, because as far as I can remember, and I have a vague memory of this, somebody else was supposed to come. My former wife's cousin was supposed to come with us, but he didn't want to because of his son. You see, both Medjesi men, the father and the son, and I didn't put their names on the list as victims at Ovcara. I couldn't remember them at first, but they were there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me: When you were taken out of the hangar, were there any other people there? Were you the last one to be taken out of the hanger or did anyone else follow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after this group of people, five or six of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I mean within this group.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone. Those of us who were taken out, I keep remembering these names. I've been remembering them for the past 15 years, and I keep saying the same thing for the past 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand my question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that the group of you, five to six people, were standing in the place that you indicated. What I'm interested in is whether you were let out of the hangar at the same time or one by one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that a witness whom we have heard from in connection with these beatings accompanied by the reservists' whistles had said that the group that he was standing with outside - and you were within that group as well - did not witness the beatings but had only heard that and had seen people perpetrating the beatings coming in and out, would you still stand by your previous statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, once I'd been beaten up, there were tears coming out of my eyes. My knees were trembling. I was bleeding, and at one point I stumbled and I let the blood fall on to the ground because I didn't want any stains to remain on my clothes because I knew I would be wearing the same clothes the next day. And I don't know what witness could have said that, but maybe he was deaf and blind and he might have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to refer to the page 3278 in the transcript and 3347. Thank you. And if I were to tell you that the witness we have heard from here said that this group which set out for Vukovar left at night-time at around 6.00, would you still claim that you left earlier?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 6.00 means total darkness. And let me just stress once again that it was sunset -- well, Mr. Vasic, it might have been a quarter past 4.00 or a 20 past 4.00, and as soon as we got to Velepromet, it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's on pages 3316 and 3317 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer. Now I have another question. When you were within the hangar and outside the hangar, you saw no JNA officers there. You've already said that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've already said that. I did not see any officers, but I saw young soldiers. And, Mr. Vasic, you can't see everything because there was a huge crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the course of your stay at Ovcara you didn't see any tractors, either within the hangar or near the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep saying: Is that right? Is that right? You're going really fast. There were some machines to the right. I know that the light wasn't very good. We even had electricity, you know, but the light bulb wasn't very good, so it was pretty dark in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether when you gave evidence before the court in Belgrade, do you remember whether you were asked about the presence of a tractor and you said that you didn't see any? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, may I tell you something about these transcripts from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we bought an ox from a Serb in Vukovar, and what it read in the transcript was that they bought a plane. You can read it in the transcript. It says so on page 6. Yeah, there was something. It could have been a bulldozer or something, but I'm not sure. There was something up but I can't remember what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the answer. I'm not trying to force you to tell me something that you don't remember. Thank you. Can you tell me: As you were standing in front of the hangar with these other people for 20 or 25 minutes, did you see if any other prisoners were taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did you say? 20, 25 minutes or what -- you mean when we were taken out?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you were taken out, as you were standing in front of the hangar, did you see if any other prisoners were taken out of the hangar during that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see our group and the Medjesi man, but he returned, he didn't want to come with us because his son was left behind, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst you were standing outside, did you see any buses arrive at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Mr. Vasic. I think not, and -- I think not 80 per cent, but mostly I don't remember, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you remember how long it took you to get from Ovcara to Velepromet and then Modateks, if you can?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Some 15 minutes it would have been normally, but in this way it took us about 25 minutes. The drive was slow because we couldn't all fit into the van properly, so we were sitting one on top of the other, and Cakalic was sitting next to the driver in the front seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was driving the van?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, Mr. Vasic. But I know that Goran Ivankovic was present. As to whether he was driving or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned you saw Tomislav Pap and you said he was the warehouse keeper at the hospital with Dr. Vesna Bosanac. What would you say if I were to tell you that Mrs. Vesna Bosanac indicated that he was a soldier when she compiled her own list? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is up to Dr. Bosanac because she's more intelligent and she probably knows better than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's Exhibit 39. May I just come back to this hangar at Ovcara for a moment. Replying to my learned friend's question, you said that the people were beaten up as they got off the bus. What I'd like to know is whether you saw whether everybody else was beaten up once you were in the hangar or do you only assume that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't guarantee that every single man was beaten up, but that people were being beaten up, and especially the ones at the end of the circle because they were coming in and looking at the crowd because they always had it in for someone, if you see what I mean. They felt hatred for someone and they wanted to hurt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So some people were particularly picked on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know why, because of their participation in some crime or because of some former personal relations or problems?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm in no position to reply to that. Some -- most of them were actually young -- younger than me, 30 years younger than me, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me conclude on Ovcara, and I'd like to move on to when you were taken to Sremska Mitrovica and my colleague will deal with the other matters. Can you tell me: When you arrived at Sremska Mitrovica, were you beaten up and did you have to run the gauntlet there as well as the same way at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I've been here for five days now, and I've always been asked: How is it going, Mr. Berghofer? And I always said: Very good, very well. But after my testimony yesterday, I had a sleepless night and I probably will have one tomorrow [as interpreted] as well, because this is really painful. These are painful memories and -- but I'm still finding it in myself. I'm still trying to summon up the strength to tell you: You didn't know where it was worse, where it was more horrific, at Ovcara, or in Mitrovica. And I'm very pleased, Mr. Vasic, that you've asked me a question about Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the gauntlet. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that very well indeed. You know, Mr. Vasic, it's not the sort of thing you can ever forget. There was a gauntlet on either side. We passed through it and were beaten in the process. The late Zeljko Bujan [phoen] dropped one of his shoes, so he went back to get it, and hen he was beaten again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I have some specific questions about this.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to finish my cross-examination by the end of the day, if I can. I'm really doing my best, but I do have several questions about this. You told us how it was over there. Did you give any statements there to any security officers, military security officers, while you were at Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, not as far as I remember, although a man called Soljic was killed right next to me. I'm really sorry that you didn't allow me to go on about that so I can tell that story, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You have my sincerest apologies, Mr. Berghofer, it's just that I'm running out of time here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You weren't interviewed and you provided no statements throughout your time there, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just signed a petition. There was some lads who were on their way to see President Tudjman so that he could have us released.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your time at Sremska Mitrovica, did you see any people from Vukovar's TO, people you knew from Vukovar? Did any of those come to Sremska Mitrovica at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure they did, Mr. Vasic. For example, Gani Jakaj [phoen], a local baker and friend of mine, Ljubo Pribudic, a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Mitrovica, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing much. They were prisoners there, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. What I'm asking you about is members of the Serbian TO from Vukovar. Did any of those people ever come to Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Vasic. I don't think I understood you the first time around. Well, you see, there was a curtain and behind the curtain there was Petar Rukalo [phoen], he was hiding there. I think his mother's maiden name was Ikac. He had taken cover behind that curtain. And then there was this man called Dzoga Jovanovic, a drummer, and the officer was asking me questions. I had to give my father's name, Baltazar. He smiled and he said: One of those cartoon characters, right? And I said: No, he's slightly bit older. He asked me about my nickname, and I said: Beli. I was a good-natured person, so I was handing out lighters, cigarette lighters, to all sorts of people from the hospital. And I faired pretty well on that day, I can say that, I think. Yet there were people who were hiding behind the curtain. And on one occasion, young Rodic turned up in uniform. He was a reserve captain. He lives three houses down the street from me, but he did not even notice me. Also, if you could help me out with this, Sokocanin [phoen], his best man, the warehouse man who got away. Can you give me a hand with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you so much for helping me out. Goran Hadzic came once, and he said -- it was stinking so badly inside because there were 154 of us in a single room and nobody could lie down on the floor. We were packed like sardines standing up. That's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Berghofer. I just have one question left, and I need to go back to something. You said you were being questioned by an officer, right? My question was: Did you give any statements or anything? So who was this officer asking you questions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was questioned on three different occasions, one of which was particularly dreadful. I have a strong voice, but when he spoke up the whole room was shaking. That's how loud he was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did any of them ever introduce themselves, told you their names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is after these -- the interrogations conducted by these officers, did you sign any statements or did they perhaps compile official notes of some sort, a record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember signing the last one I told you about. But guess what he asked me: How many Serbs were killed in your cellar? That was a question he asked me. And I replied: Can you please repeat that question? And he said: How many Serbs were killed in your cellar? And I said: Sir, thank you very much. To my great fortunate, none at all. And he said: I didn't say you necessarily, but who did? Mr. Vasic, at this point he told me: We have other ways of interrogating people. You know that? At this point, I was nearly fainting with fear, but the man didn't even touch me, as opposed to the one previously at Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems that time is up now. I just have one subject to cover. I think I won't take more than 10 or 15 minutes at the very most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Well, we've reached the time when we must adjourn today. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning, and hopefully we will finish Mr. Berghofer's evidence in the course of tomorrow. We will now adjourn.
